name: nc
description: netcat: reads and writes raw data over TCP or UDP — the "Swiss Army knife" for testing ports, probing services, and moving data.

flags.description: Zero-I/O mode: just scan whether the port is open.
Listen mode (server side); -lp PORT to specify the port.
Execute a program after connecting (traditional nc; not in OpenBSD nc).

examples.explanation: Instant port check — is the HTTPS port reachable from here? The minimal connectivity test for a specific service.
Bash built-in alternative (no nc needed): succeeds silently if the port is open.
Speaks raw HTTP to a server — the classic way to inspect protocol behavior without curl.
On machine B: listens and saves. On machine A: nc B_IP 9999 < file.txt — a one-line file transfer.

about: nc variants differ: OpenBSD nc (most common on modern Linux) has no -e; GNU netcat and ncat (from Nmap) do. ncat adds SSL (-ssl) support. Despite its power for testing, nc on untrusted networks is plaintext — never use it for sensitive data.
useCases: Test whether a TCP/UDP port is open.
Quick data transfer between trusted machines.
mistakes: Expecting -e on OpenBSD nc — use ncat or a FIFO instead.
Sending sensitive data over plaintext nc sessions.
warnings: nc -l binds a listening port that anyone on the network can connect to; never expose it beyond trusted networks.
